title: From Hormuz to Beijing — Eddie Would Go

u.Cómo la guerra de Irán está reordenando: How Iran's war is reordering the world's energy dependencies
u.El cierre del Estrecho de Ormuz se prese: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is presented, in some strategic circles, as a calculated move to check China's rise. The data from the first weeks suggest exactly the opposite: the largest energy disruption in modern history is the best possible advertisement for the Chinese clean technology industry. Escaping Arab oil has a price. And for now, that price is called Beijing. But history rarely allows itself to be reduced to a single irony. Behind that first layer of analysis there are minerals, there are Gulf actors absent from the narrative, and there are counterarguments deserving more space than they usually receive.
u.«La invencibilidad depende de uno mismo;: «Invincibility depends on oneself; the enemy's vulnerability depends on him.»
u.— Sun Tzu, El arte de la guerra, Capítul: — Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Chapter IV (Tactical Dispositions)
u.El 28 de febrero de 2026, cuando los pri: On 28 February 2026, when the first American and Israeli missiles struck installations on Iranian territory, Brent crude was trading at around 63 dollars a barrel. Within less than a week it had passed 92. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passes — triggered what the International Energy Agency described as «the greatest global energy security challenge in history».[7] Queues at petrol stations returned to Europe, more from fear than from any shortage of supply. In India, liquefied gas began to run short. Singapore and South Korea launched emergency energy-saving campaigns. The world remembered, once again, just how tied it remains to fossil fuels.
u.En algunos despachos de Washington, el i: In certain offices in Washington, the outbreak of the conflict generated not only urgency but a degree of strategic satisfaction. The argument, circulated discreetly among analysts sympathetic to the Trump administration, ran as follows: a severe disruption of oil and LNG supply hits China — the world's largest importer of both — disproportionately hard. Depriving Beijing of cheap energy amounts to slowing its factories and its growth. It is, in short, geopolitical competition by other means. Meanwhile the United States has become a fossil resource export power.
u.Ocho semanas después del inicio del conf: Eight weeks after the conflict began, the data indicate that this calculation was wrong. Not partially: radically. The war some in Washington conceived as a blow to China's rise may end up being a major catalyst of Beijing's economic power. But this analysis cannot stop there. Because the thesis of the «Chinese electrostate as net winner» is so seductive that it risks replicating the very vice it denounces: substituting one simple narrative for another. The reality that emerges is richer, more contradictory and more uncomfortable than either of the two competing narratives.
u.La formulación más clara de la tesis dom: The clearest formulation of the dominant thesis comes from the economist Paul Krugman, who published in early April an article titled "Chinese Electrotech is the Big Winner in the Iran War".[1] The argument is, on the face of it, counterintuitive: China is the world's largest oil importer. A supply shock in crude markets ought to hit it head on. And yet Krugman maintains that it will emerge strengthened, because the Iran war functions as a gigantic advertisement for the products China makes better than anyone: solar panels, lithium-ion batteries, electric vehicles, wind turbines.
u.La lógica es simple. Cuando el precio de: The logic is simple. When fossil fuel prices spike, the electric alternative becomes even more attractive. The countries most dependent on imported oil and gas have the most urgent incentive to accelerate their transition. Sam Butler-Sloss, research director at Ember, sums it up precisely: «High fossil prices drive the shift, making already cheap electrotech even more competitive. With electrification, nations have for the first time the tools to eliminate imported fuels entirely». Fatih Birol, executive director of the IEA, was equally direct with The Guardian: the damage to confidence in fossil fuels «is permanent», with «permanent consequences for global energy markets».[3]
u.China a esto sumó una comprensión muy cl: To this China added a very clear understanding of its limitations, weaknesses and strengths: during the years of calm, Beijing built oil reserves robust enough to ride out this crisis.
u.Los datos de las primeras semanas del co: The data from the first weeks of the conflict corroborate the main lines of the thesis. According to Ember, Chinese solar technology exports hit a record in the first month of the crisis.[11] Foreign sales of Chinese electric and hybrid vehicles grew 140% year on year, according to the China Passenger Car Association.[9] Lithium-ion battery exports rose 50.4% in the first quarter of 2026.[12] The WilderHill Clean Energy ETF climbed 118% in a single month.[14] Taken together, the numbers paint a coherent picture. The problem, as we shall see, is that the picture is incomplete.
u.Para entender por qué la tesis tiene pes: To understand why the thesis carries weight, it is worth pausing on the Spanish case as an example. Spain is not merely a model of renewable energy policy: it is, at this moment, the clearest natural experiment in what it means to have bet on electrification before the shock arrived.
u.En 2019, el gas fijaba el precio de la e: In 2019, gas set the price of Spanish electricity in 75% of the hours of the day. In 2026, that figure will have fallen to 15% — the sharpest reduction among Europe's large gas-dependent markets.[5] The result is observable in spot prices: while Germany and Italy pay more than a hundred euros per megawatt-hour, Spain moves between 37 and 57.[8] There are episodes in which the price falls to zero — or to negative values — during hours of peak solar production. It is the direct consequence of having built, years in advance, the infrastructure that today acts as a shield, and of having diversified supply away from the Persian Gulf towards North Africa, in particular Algeria. Spain imports 38% of its gas from Algeria, which partially insulated it from the most severe shock associated with the closure of the Strait.
u.El ministro de Economía, Carlos Cuerpo,: The Economy Minister, Carlos Cuerpo, summed it up to CNBC: Spain was «better prepared for this crisis» thanks to the transition towards renewables, which had reduced its exposure to shocks and increased its «energy sovereignty».[6] The phrase deserves quoting in full because it captures something important: the energy transition is not only a climate policy. It is, in this context, a national security policy. Every megawatt of solar or wind capacity installed before the conflict is, today, a shield against the volatility of the Persian Gulf.
The pattern repeats beyond Spain. Portugal and the Nordic countries have registered the lowest electricity prices in the European Union since the conflict began. Ethiopia, which generates 95% of its electricity from hydropower, is accelerating the transition to electric mobility to reduce its dependence on imported oil. Pakistan, which began importing Chinese solar panels en masse three years ago, has absorbed the shock considerably better than its neighbours.[9] The message is consistent: the greater the prior electrification, the lower the vulnerability to the fossil fuel shock.
u.Y sin embargo, hay que resistir la tenta: And yet one must resist the temptation to universalise the Spanish case. Spain combines conditions that make it exceptionally resistant to this particular kind of shock: a peninsular geography that limits electrical interconnection with the rest of Europe — which, paradoxically, forced it to develop self-sufficiency — an energy mix with renewable penetration unmatched among the large European economies, and a gas dependence that has always been covered in greater proportion by Algerian LNG than by Gulf supplies. The seventy-five percentage point difference in gas exposure between Spain and Italy is not achieved in a week: it is the result of sustained investment over more than a decade. To present the Spanish case as an attainable norm is, to say the least, premature.
u.Si la tesis es correcta —si la guerra de: If the thesis is correct — if the Iran war is structurally accelerating the global energy transition — the most relevant geopolitical question is not how high crude rises. It is who makes the substitutes. And the answer, uncomfortable as it may be, is: China.
u.No en parte. De forma aplastante. Según: Not partly. Overwhelmingly. According to data from Foreign Policy and the IEA, China controls more than 80% of world manufacturing capacity for solar panels, wind turbines and batteries.[11] It processes the great majority of the critical minerals needed for those technologies. More than half the cars sold in China in 2026 will be electric — the result of decades of deliberate industrial policy oriented as much to energy security as to reducing carbon emissions.[13] As well as price dumping policies and strategies for eliminating foreign competitors who lack the backing of the government in Beijing.
u.Ember, en un informe de diciembre de 202: Ember, in a December 2025 report, coined the term «electrostate» to describe China as the first major economy in which electric technologies became the dominant engine of energy growth, and was blunt in its diagnosis: «China is not merely manufacturing electrotech hardware. It is manufacturing an energy future in which it occupies a dominant position».[11]
u.La analista Alicia García Herrero, de Br: The analyst Alicia García Herrero, of Bruegel, put it with equal precision: «China has a great deal of power because it is protected from the shock while the rest of the world is not».[12] China's clean energy industry — solar, batteries, electric vehicles — accounted for more than 11% of Chinese GDP in 2025 and more than a third of its growth. According to Ember data, in 2024 investment and production in clean energy contributed the equivalent of 10% of Chinese GDP, and the sector grew three times faster than the economy as a whole. Chinese firms already account for 75% of world patent applications in clean energy technology, against 5% in the year 2000. To sustain that expansion, China needs foreign demand. The Iran shock is providing it massively and unexpectedly.
u.Al mismo tiempo que los Estados Unidos,: At the same time, the United States, and the Trump government, are abandoning any attempt to remain current or relevant in this process.
u.La reconfiguración geopolítica ya está e: The geopolitical reconfiguration is already under way. Canada partially lifted its restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles. Several European leaders travelled to Beijing to sign clean energy cooperation agreements. «China has gone from being perceived as a cheap supplier to being treated as a long-term strategic partner in the energy transition», wrote Jeong Won Kim, of the Energy Studies Institute at the National University of Singapore.[9]
u.El analista Zhao Xiuye, de China-US Focu: The analyst Zhao Xiuye, of China-US Focus, puts it this way: «For countries dependent on imported oil, disruptions in the global energy supply have made China's renewable energy strategy more attractive».[16] Foreign Policy adds an element that complicates the picture further: by starting the war without consulting its allies, Washington has reinforced the perception that the United States is today the largest source of geopolitical volatility, while China presents itself as a more stable trading partner. The conclusion that follows from that analysis is uncomfortable: «the war some conceived as a blow to China's rise may end up being the greatest catalyst of Beijing's economic power in a generation».[11]
u.La otra dependencia: el problema de los: The other dependence: the critical minerals problem
u.Hasta aquí, el argumento fluye con elega: So far the argument flows elegantly. But there is one piece the dominant thesis tends to treat with excessive simplicity and which, once examined in detail, considerably complicates the picture: the supply chain of the critical minerals that make clean technology possible.
u.Litio, cobalto, grafito, níquel, mangane: Lithium, cobalt, graphite, nickel, manganese, rare earths, copper. These are the materials without which no lithium-ion battery, electric motor, wind turbine or functional solar panel exists. And the map of their extraction, refining and processing shows a geographical concentration that, in some segments, exceeds that of Persian Gulf oil itself. According to Goldman Sachs data, China refines 68% of the world's cobalt, 65% of its nickel and 60% of the lithium needed for electric vehicle batteries. It controls between 85 and 90% of rare earth refining and 92% of rare earth magnet manufacturing. Seventy-five per cent of all the world's batteries and most electric vehicles are made in China.
u.La proyección a mediano plazo es aún más: The medium-term projection is even more revealing. By 2035, according to the Overseas Development Institute, China projects supplying more than 60% of refined lithium and cobalt globally, around 80% of battery-grade graphite and rare earth elements, and approximately 70% of battery-grade manganese.
u.Con lo cual aunque la UE y USA, pueden c: So although the EU and the US can obtain supplies of these metals from elsewhere — Chile, Australia, Indonesia or Brazil — reactivating or developing the industrial process for treating these elements will take longer than simply securing the raw material; China retains its dominance in the key segments of the value chain, particularly in processing and refining. The conclusion that follows is structural: electrification resolves one geopolitical dependence — that on Persian Gulf oil — and simultaneously consolidates another: that on Chinese refining and processing of the materials that make it possible.
u.El problema no es solo la concentración: The problem is not only the current concentration. It is the time it takes to change it. Unlike oil, where a new field can come into production in three to five years, critical minerals have a radically different investment profile. The average development time for a new copper mine — the metal whose demand will grow 30% by 2040 according to the IEA — is more than 10 years from discovery to commercial production. For lithium, the IEA projects a 40% shortfall in mined supply relative to demand in 2035 under stated policy scenarios. For copper, the shortfall is 30%. Even assuming that the countries dependent today on Gulf oil decide to accelerate their electrification massively as a result of this conflict, the supply chain for the materials that electrification requires cannot scale in months, or in a few years.
u.El Outlook de Minerales Críticos 2025 de: The IEA's Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 introduces a further data point that illuminates the system's structural fragility: if the largest supplier of each mineral is removed from planning scenarios — that is, if China stops supplying graphite, rare earths or refined lithium — the remaining supply would cover barely 35% to 40% of projected demand for graphite and rare earths in 2035. For battery-grade nickel, coverage would be below 55%. In other words: the global energy transition system is built on a supply chain that, in its most critical links, has no available substitute within the relevant horizon.
u.Aquí hay una ironía adicional que el deb: There is a further irony here that the usual debate on the energy transition tends to subsume. Sam Butler-Sloss, of Ember, formulated the central argument for electrification precisely: «Fossil fuel prices are, in essence, a geopolitical tax». The phrase is fair. But if the critical minerals for electrification are concentrated in a single geography with even greater intensity than oil, then the relevant question is not whether a geopolitical tax exists, but to whom it is paid. And the answer, in the accelerated transition scenario the Iran war is sketching, is that the tax shifts from the Persian Gulf to Chinese refining and processing chains. The solar panel already installed cannot be «switched off» by Beijing, as defenders of electrification point out. But the lithium that has not yet reached the German factory can indeed be subject to Chinese export policy, as was already seen with germanium and gallium in earlier trade conflicts.
u.Existe, en este punto, una paradoja adic: There is, at this point, an additional paradox that market dynamics have introduced inadvertently. China's own dominance in battery mineral production has generated, over the last two years, an extraordinary fall in prices: lithium dropped more than 80% from its 2022 peaks, and graphite and cobalt also fell between 10% and 20% in 2024. That deflation, a direct result of Chinese scale, is discouraging investment in diversification. The IEA records that growth in critical minerals investment fell to 2% in real terms in 2024, against 14% in 2023. New projects in countries other than China find financing ever harder when the reference price is set by a producer operating with subsidies, economies of scale and long-term strategic objectives not subject to the logic of short-term returns. China, in other words, does not merely dominate the current supply of critical minerals: its own production conditions are inhibiting the investment that would reduce that future dependence.
u.Aquí hay una ironía estratégica de prime: Here lies a strategic irony of the first order. One hypothesis that circulated in certain foreign policy circles during preparations for the attack on Iran was that a severe disruption of the global energy market would disproportionately affect China. The logic: China imports more than ten million barrels of oil a day and depends on the Strait of Hormuz for a significant fraction of that volume. A shock in crude prices would raise its industrial costs, slow its growth and weaken it in the technological and economic contest with the West. The Iran war, on that reading, was not only an operation against Tehran.
u.Los datos de las ocho primeras semanas s: The data from the first eight weeks suggest that calculation underestimated two factors. The first is the degree of relative insulation China has built against the fossil shock. More than 30% of its final energy consumption already comes from electricity — the highest share among the large economies, exceeding the United States by almost ten percentage points.[16] The second is that even the countries that do suffer the shock — Japan, South Korea, the European economies, Southeast Asia — react by accelerating the transition, which expands demand for Chinese products. Every government that announces emergency incentives for electric vehicles, every company that installs solar panels in the face of gas price uncertainty, is in practice a new customer for the Chinese supply chain.
u.Foreign Policy señala un elemento que co: Foreign Policy points to an element that complicates the strategic picture further: by starting the war without consulting its allies, Washington has reinforced the perception that the United States is today the greatest source of geopolitical volatility, while China presents itself as a more stable trading partner.[11] In that context, depending on Beijing to acquire clean technology begins to look, comparatively, like the lesser of the available risks. It is a conclusion that would have seemed extraordinary barely five years ago. Today, in the corridors of foreign ministries from Jakarta to Nairobi, by way of Mexico City and Warsaw, the phrase is heard with increasing frequency and ease.
u.Los actores invisibles: el Golfo en reco: The invisible actors: the Gulf in reconfiguration
u.El relato Washington-Pekín que estructur: The Washington-Beijing narrative structuring most of the available analysis of the war's energy consequences has a considerable blind spot: the Gulf countries themselves. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait and Iraq are not passive actors in this story. They are, simultaneously, the principal victims of the shock, the most urgently pressed to rethink their economic model and, in all probability, the next mass customers for Chinese clean technology. Their absence from the dominant analysis is no minor detail: it is an omission that distorts the map of forces.
u.La magnitud del daño al modelo económico: The magnitude of the damage to the Gulf's economic model is hard to exaggerate. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused what the Atlantic Council described as «a systemic collapse of the Gulf Cooperation Council's economic model». Crude production in Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Kuwait and Iraq fell collectively by more than 14 million barrels a day. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on all its LNG exports. The Strait is not only the exit route for Gulf oil and gas: it is also where more than 80% of the region's food imports enter. Before anyone had even begun to talk about energy transition, Gulf governments were managing a food emergency. Doha, Dubai, Manama and Kuwait City depend entirely or almost entirely on desalination for drinking water, and those installations consume enormous quantities of energy. The disruption was total, in a sense that goes far beyond hydrocarbon markets.
u.Y sin embargo, lo que hace este escenari: And yet what makes this scenario analytically interesting is not only the present damage. It is the reorientation that damage precipitates. Saudi Arabia had Vision 2030 before this war. The Emirates had built Barakah — the first Arab nuclear plant in operation — had hosted COP28 in Dubai and were already exploring the possibility of a second nuclear plant. Masdar, Abu Dhabi's renewable energy company, is one of the largest investors in renewables outside China. In January 2025, Masdar and the utility EWEC announced the construction of a 5.2 gigawatt solar plant with 19 gigawatt-hours of battery storage, capable of supplying one gigawatt of continuous capacity. Saudi Arabia is developing at Neom the world's largest green hydrogen project, with production due to begin at the end of 2026.
u.La guerra no destruye esos planes. Los a: The war does not destroy those plans. It accelerates them, with an urgency that was previously strategic and is now existential. And to execute them, the Gulf countries need technology. The cheapest, most available and most mature technology for solar panels, battery storage and electric vehicles is, overwhelmingly, Chinese technology. The same logic that applies to Germany, Japan or South Korea also applies to Saudi Arabia and the Emirates: the shock that destroys their rentier model is also the most powerful incentive to accelerate a transition that will turn them into mass buyers of Chinese electrotech. There is something deeply ironic in this outcome: the countries whose export collapse is the cause of the global shock may end up being, via their own energy reorientation, one more vector consolidating Chinese industrial dominance.
u.Hay un dato geográfico que ilustra los l: There is a geographical fact that illustrates the limits of the Gulf's resilience against its own vulnerability. Saudi Arabia has the East-West pipeline, which can carry up to 5 million barrels a day from its eastern fields to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz. The Emirates have the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline, with a capacity of 1.5 million barrels a day. Together they do not exceed 6.5 million barrels a day, far below the more than 20 million barrels that transited the Strait before the conflict. The geography of the Gulf has no short-term engineering solution. And that structural limitation is also a powerful argument for the oil producers themselves to accelerate diversification towards energy sources that do not depend on navigable straits.
u.No sería riguroso presentar el conjunto: It would not be rigorous to present this analysis as though the conclusions were already settled. They are not. The thesis of the Chinese electrostate as net winner of the Iran war is, at best, a robust hypothesis backed by data. It has cracks, and some are significant.
u.El Atlantic Council señala que, en teorí: The Atlantic Council notes that, in theory, high fossil fuel prices should accelerate electrification; in practice, the immediate pressure on households and industry tends to shift political attention towards emergency measures — fuel subsidies, tax reductions, price controls — that do not transform the energy structure and sometimes reinforce it.[17] Spain itself, presented as a model of renewable resilience, approved a €5 billion package of tax cuts that included a reduction in VAT on fossil fuels.[14] Short-term urgency sits badly with long-term investment. This pattern has sharp historical precedents: after the 1973 oil shock, Western governments announced energy efficiency and substitution programmes. Many of those programmes were cancelled or diluted when the crude price fell again. The question of whether this time is different cannot be answered from inside the shock.
u.Gonzalo Escribano, del Instituto Elcano,: Gonzalo Escribano, of the Elcano Institute, adds another nuance that transitional optimism tends to overlook: there is a real risk that coal experiences a temporary return as an emergency response in some countries, which would transitorily slow the transition.[15] Germany already travelled that road after the Russian invasion of Ukraine: it temporarily reactivated coal plants that were being phased out. The political logic of an energy emergency is frequently that of the path of least resistance, and coal — abundant, cheap, with infrastructure already installed — is exactly that. In the United States, the Trump administration has not used the crisis to accelerate electrification but for precisely the opposite: as a lever to dismantle climate regulations and justify the domestic expansion of fossil fuels.[21] The American exception is no marginal detail: Washington is the world's second largest economy and its model of response to the shock has implications for the global carbon price, the relative competitiveness of renewables and other countries' willingness to bear transition costs.
u.Pero la fisura más profunda de la tesis: But the deepest crack in the thesis — and the least frequently articulated — has to do with the nature of the Chinese electrostate itself. Researchers at Harvard University recently formulated a distinction that deserves attention: China has adopted renewables, but that is not equivalent to a «transition» in the sense Western analysts usually give the term. The difference matters. China is building renewable capacity at a speed without historical precedent; simultaneously, it continues building coal plants. Coal accounts for more than 55% of Chinese electricity generation, and in 2025 installed coal capacity in China will continue to grow. The strategy is not to substitute renewables for coal: it is to add renewables on top of a fossil base that is not shrinking, at least not in the short term.
u.El Centre for Research on Energy and Cle: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air published in February 2026 an analysis that directly challenges the narrative of the electrostate as a climatically coherent actor: China will not meet its own 14th Five-Year Plan targets. Specifically, it will not achieve the target of reducing carbon emissions per unit of GDP, nor the commitments to «strictly control» growth in coal consumption and the construction of new coal plants. And most significantly: in its new Nationally Determined Contribution, China omitted the commitment to gradually reduce coal consumption over the 2026-2030 period. CREA's analysts note that this raises the risk of an emissions rebound after the relative stability of the last two years. The «electrostate» is therefore also, simultaneously, the planet's largest consumer and largest producer of coal. Both things are true at once, and any analysis that picks one of the two on which to build its narrative is making an editorial selection, not a complete description.
u.El otro talón de Aquiles de esta tesis e: The other Achilles heel of this thesis is that the manufacture of chips essential to the electrification process depends, among other things, on helium exports through the Strait of Hormuz, so the conflict's impacts will also affect the production capacity even of the electrical powers.
u.La historia ofrece aquí un paralelo que: History offers here a parallel worth examining closely, because it illuminates both the possibilities and the limits of the present moment. The oil shocks of the 1970s — the OPEC embargo of 1973 and the Iranian revolution of 1979 — generated exactly the same substitution impulse we see today, but with the only technology available at scale then: nuclear power. The response was massive and sustained. France announced the Messmer Plan in March 1974: 51 reactors in a decade, with the explicit goal of generating most of its electricity without depending on imported oil.[23] Japan, which in 1973 generated 66% of its electricity from Persian Gulf oil, made nuclear expansion a national strategic priority and went from five reactors in operation in 1973 to 54 in 2010, providing close to 30% of its electricity.[24] In the United States, 31 of the 47 reactors inaugurated in the 1980s had begun construction after the first shock of 1973.[23] The logic was the same as today's: substitute a dangerous energy dependence with a technology offering autonomy from Persian Gulf volatility.
u.Durante casi una década, el plan pareció: For almost a decade, the plan seemed to work. Then the bills came in. On 28 March 1979 — less than two months after Khomeini's triumph in Tehran — a valve failure at Three Mile Island, in Pennsylvania, caused a partial meltdown of the reactor core. There were no direct casualties, but the panic was total and the political reaction immediate. Between 1980 and 1984, 52 nuclear reactors were cancelled in the United States.[25] In 1986, the explosion of reactor number four at Chernobyl marked the end of nuclear expansion as a systematic response to fossil shocks. Fukushima, in 2011, was the third act: Japan, the country that had bet most heavily on nuclear fission to escape Arab oil, abruptly shut down almost its entire nuclear fleet and returned to importing liquefied natural gas at emergency prices. The alternative that markets and governments had chosen in order to free themselves from oil carried with it catastrophic risks that, at the moment of the wager, nobody had known — or wanted — to calculate at their true magnitude.
u.El paralelo con el momento actual no es: The parallel with the present moment is not exact, but it is deeply instructive. Solar and wind energy do not have the catastrophic risk profile of nuclear fission: a solar panel cannot melt down or contaminate a region for decades. But the history of the 1970s teaches two things this analysis would do well to retain. The first: that fossil shocks do produce structural and durable energy reorientations, not merely emergency rhetoric. The nuclear boom was real, massive and sustained for years; the energy efficiency investments of the 1970s and 1980s permanently changed the energy intensity of Western economies. There are reasons to believe the present impulse is equally real. The second: that every energy alternative brings its own risks, some invisible at the moment of the wager. In the 1970s, nobody imagined Chernobyl while signing the Messmer Plan contracts. Today, technological dependence on China for the entire supply chain — from lithium refining to the manufacture of solar inverters — is the risk that the urgency of the moment tends to minimise or accept too readily.
u.Los analistas más optimistas argumentan: The more optimistic analysts argue that this time the cost structure has already changed deeply enough for the effect to be permanent: renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels in the great majority of new projects, with or without a crisis.[4] The argument is valid, but the history of the 1970s suggests that costs are not the only determinant of energy trajectories. Politics, national security, industrial interests, infrastructure inertia and unpredictable accidents — Three Mile Island was a valve failure, not a systemic one — also shape the path. The cheapness of renewables is a necessary condition for the transition, but it is not sufficient to guarantee it.
u.El ganador provisional, y las preguntas: The provisional winner, and the questions that remain
u.Lo que sí parece claro, con independenci: What does seem clear, regardless of how long the conflict lasts, is the provisional geography of the beneficiary. In a few weeks the world has received a reminder about the fragility of the fossil resource supply chain. The perception of risk — which economists know moves capital as much as prices do — has changed durably. And on that new map of risks, China occupies two positions simultaneously: it is the supplier of the most visible alternative, and it is the bottleneck of the mineral chain that makes that alternative possible. Both are strategic advantages. Their coexistence is what makes the Chinese position so difficult to counter within the relevant horizon.
u.La ironía es considerable, y llega en ca: The irony is considerable, and it comes in layers. The war initiated by Washington and Tel Aviv has ended up reinforcing Beijing's strategic position in the energy sphere. The Persian Gulf countries, whose rentier model is crumbling, are being pushed towards a transition that turns them into potential mass buyers of Chinese technology. The European countries suffering the shock were already seeking a substitute for Russian gas two years before this war; now they have a second argument of urgency. The economies of Southeast Asia, highly dependent on imported oil, today have the clearest structural incentive in their history to electrify. And each of those movements leads, in the current state of the global value chain, in the same direction.
u.Y sin embargo, tres preguntas fundamenta: And yet three fundamental questions remain open, and no honest analysis can dodge them. The first: how much of what we are observing is a structural and permanent reorientation, and how much is the noise of a market in shock that will correct when prices normalise? The oil shocks of the 1970s produced real substitution impulses; they also produced reversals when crude fell. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens, if the barrel returns to 70 dollars, the political urgency that today pushes governments towards electrification may fade with equal speed. There is no guarantee it will not.
u.La segunda pregunta: ¿es la dependencia: The second question: is dependence on Chinese technology really more manageable than dependence on Gulf oil? The strongest argument in favour of electrification is that a solar panel already installed on a German roof cannot be «switched off» by Xi Jinping in the way a tanker can be blocked in the Strait of Hormuz. That is true. But the lithium that has not yet left the Congolese mine, the graphite that has not passed through Chinese processing facilities, the wind turbine that has not reached the port of Hamburg — all of that can indeed be subject to export restrictions, tariffs or political conditions. China has done it before with germanium and gallium. The question is not whether that second dependence exists, but whether it is more manageable than the first over the long term. The honest answer is that we do not yet know.
u.La tercera pregunta es quizás la más inc: The third question is perhaps the most uncomfortable: can the world electrify fast enough for the transition to outrun the scarcity of minerals? The shortfalls the IEA projects for lithium and copper in 2035 are not marginal bottlenecks: they are physical limitations in the supply chain of global electrification. If demand for critical minerals grows at the rate accelerated transition scenarios require, and if investment in new mining and refining capacity does not scale at the same speed — something the current context of low prices makes less, not more, likely — the result will not merely be a delay in the transition. It will be a new form of energy dependence, this time expressed in tonnes of cobalt and kilograms of graphite instead of barrels of oil.
u.El electroestado chino no es una promesa: The Chinese electrostate is not an ideological promise. It is, for the moment, the only industrial reality available to supply the scale of transition the crisis is demanding. And the Iran war, with all its tragedy, may have been the catalyst that makes that reality irreversible. But irreversible does not mean without consequences, or without risks, or without counterarguments. If the history of energy shocks teaches anything — from the 1973 embargo to Fukushima — it is that great energy substitution wagers always come with risks that only become visible when it is too late not to have paid them. This time, those who make the substitutes are the same ones who process the minerals without which those substitutes do not exist. That does not invalidate the transition. But it does oblige us to go in with our eyes open.
